title: Unit 1: Kinematics

topics.name: Position, velocity, and acceleration with calculus
Motion in two dimensions and projectiles

guide.title: Kinematics: review guide
guide.intro: Kinematics describes motion without asking what causes it. In Physics C you connect position, velocity, and acceleration with derivatives and integrals, in one and two dimensions.
guide.equationNote: g = 10 m/s² unless a question gives another value. Signs give direction along an axis.

sections.title: Position, velocity, and acceleration with calculus
body: Velocity is the rate of change of position, v = dx/dt, and acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, a = dv/dt = d²x/dt². Going the other way, integrate: Δx = ∫v dt and Δv = ∫a dt, then add the initial values.
The constant-acceleration equations are a special case: v = v₀ + at, x = x₀ + v₀t + ½at², and v² = v₀² + 2aΔx. Use them only when a is constant.
points: Displacement is the change in position. Distance traveled adds up every part of the path, so split the time interval wherever v changes sign.
Average velocity is Δx/Δt; average speed is distance/Δt.
An object speeds up when v and a have the same sign and slows down when they have opposite signs.

sections.title: Motion graphs and changing acceleration
body: On an x–t graph the slope is velocity. On a v–t graph the slope is acceleration, and the signed area under the curve is displacement. On an a–t graph the area is the change in velocity.

When acceleration depends on velocity, as with a resistive force giving a = −kv, separate the variables: dv/v = −k dt gives v = v₀e^(−kt). The speed decreases exponentially and never quite reaches zero.
points: Area below the time axis on a v–t graph counts as negative displacement.
Where an x–t graph has a horizontal tangent, the object is momentarily at rest.
Check units: the area under a v–t graph is in meters.

sections.title: Motion in two dimensions and projectiles
body: In two dimensions, treat x and y separately: r(t) = (x(t), y(t)), v = dr/dt, and a = dv/dt. Speed is the magnitude √(v_x² + v_y²).
A projectile with no air resistance has a_x = 0 and a_y = −g. Its horizontal velocity stays constant, and its time in the air is set by the vertical motion alone.
points: Launch speed v₀ at angle θ above the horizontal: v_x = v₀ cos θ and v_y = v₀ sin θ.
At the top of the path v_y = 0, but v_x is not zero.
Maximum height above the launch point is v_y²/(2g), using only the vertical component.

example.prompt: A particle's velocity is v(t) = 3t² − 12 m/s, and it is at x = 4 m at t = 0. Find its position at t = 3 s and the distance it travels from t = 0 to t = 3 s.

misconceptions: At the top of a throw v = 0, but a = −g.
They differ whenever the object turns around.
“A projectile's horizontal speed changes during its flight.”
With no air resistance nothing acts horizontally, so v_x stays constant.
Use calculus when the acceleration changes with time or with velocity.

questions.prompt: A particle's position is x(t) = 3t² − 2t + 1, with x in meters and t in seconds. What is its velocity at t = 2 s?
choiceExplanations: 9 is x(2), the position, not the velocity.
6 m/s² is the acceleration, d²x/dt².
12 is 6t at t = 2; the −2 from differentiating −2t was left out.

questions.prompt: An object's acceleration is a(t) = 6t m/s², and its velocity at t = 0 is 2 m/s. What is its velocity at t = 2 s?
questions.explanation: v(t) = v₀ + ∫₀ᵗ 6s ds = 2 + 3t², so v(2) = 2 + 12 = 14 m/s.
choiceExplanations: 12 m/s is the change in velocity, 3t²; the initial 2 m/s must be added.
26 m/s integrates 6t as 6t² instead of 3t².
The acceleration is not zero, so the velocity changes.

questions.prompt: An object moves along a line with velocity v(t) = 4 − 2t m/s. How far does it travel, in total, from t = 0 to t = 3 s?
questions.explanation: v = 0 at t = 2 s, so split the interval. From 0 to 2 s: ∫(4 − 2t) dt = 4 m forward. From 2 to 3 s: ∫(4 − 2t) dt = −1 m (back 1 m). Distance = 4 + 1 = 5 m.
choiceExplanations: 3 m is the displacement, 4 − 1; distance counts the 1 m traveled backward too.
4 m stops counting when the object turns around at t = 2 s.
−2 m/s is the velocity at t = 3 s, not a distance.

questions.prompt: On a graph of velocity against time, what does the signed area between the graph and the time axis represent?
choices: The distance from the starting point at every instant
questions.explanation: Displacement is ∫v dt, which is the signed area under the v–t graph.
choiceExplanations: Acceleration is the slope of the v–t graph, not the area under it.
The area gives the total displacement over the interval, not a separate distance at every instant.
Average velocity is the area divided by the time interval.

questions.prompt: A puck slides with acceleration a = −kv, where k is a positive constant, starting with speed v₀. Which expression gives its velocity v(t)?
questions.explanation: dv/dt = −kv. Separate: dv/v = −k dt, so ln(v/v₀) = −kt and v = v₀e^(−kt).
choiceExplanations: v₀ − kt would mean a constant acceleration −k, but here the acceleration depends on v.
v₀/(1 + kt) solves dv/dt = −kv², a different resistive force.
A positive exponent would make the speed grow; the force opposes the motion.

questions.prompt: A particle's position is x(t) = t³ − 6t² meters. At t = 1 s, is it speeding up or slowing down?
choices: Speeding up, because v and a are both negative
Slowing down, because the acceleration is negative
Slowing down, because the velocity is negative
Neither, because it is at rest
questions.explanation: v = 3t² − 12t, so v(1) = −9 m/s. a = 6t − 12, so a(1) = −6 m/s². They have the same sign, so the speed is increasing.
choiceExplanations: A negative acceleration slows an object only if its velocity is positive; here both are negative.
Speeding up or slowing down depends on whether v and a have the same sign, not on the sign of v alone.
v(1) = −9 m/s, so the particle is moving.

questions.prompt: A ball is thrown horizontally at 12 m/s from the top of a 20 m cliff. How far from the base of the cliff does it land? (g = 10 m/s², no air resistance)
questions.explanation: Vertical: 20 = ½(10)t², so t = 2.0 s. Horizontal: x = (12 m/s)(2.0 s) = 24 m.
choiceExplanations: 12 m uses a time of 1 s; falling 20 m takes 2.0 s.
20 m is the cliff's height, not the horizontal distance.
48 m uses t = 2h/g = 4 s; the time is the square root, √(2h/g) = 2 s.

questions.prompt: A particle's position is r(t) = (2t, t²) meters. What is its speed at t = 3 s?
choiceExplanations: 8.0 adds the components; speed is the magnitude √(v_x² + v_y²).
6.0 m/s is only the y-component.
40 is v_x² + v_y²; the square root is still needed.

questions.prompt: A projectile is launched at 30 m/s at 53° above the horizontal (sin 53° = 0.80, cos 53° = 0.60) over level ground. How high above the launch point does it rise? (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.explanation: Only the vertical component matters: v_y = 30 × 0.80 = 24 m/s. At the top v_y = 0, so H = v_y²/(2g) = 576/20 = 28.8 m.
choiceExplanations: 45 m uses the full launch speed; only the vertical component is slowed by gravity.
16.2 m uses the horizontal component, 18 m/s.
57.6 m is v_y²/g; the factor ½ (the 2 in 2g) was left out.

questions.prompt: A particle's position is x(t) = t³ − 6t² + 9t meters. What is its average velocity from t = 0 to t = 2 s?
choiceExplanations: 3 m/s is the average speed: the particle goes 4 m forward to x = 4 at t = 1 s, then 2 m back, 6 m in 2 s.
−3 m/s is the instantaneous velocity at t = 2 s, v = 3t² − 12t + 9.
2 m is the displacement; it still has to be divided by the 2 s interval.
